title: Deploy it
summary: From an empty VM to collectors running on a schedule: the stack, its secrets, the runner's token, the first scope apply and the schedule.

steps.title: What you need
narration: You need a VM with Docker and four gigabytes of memory, a DNS name for it, and your private compliance repo.
Two repositories are involved. The public Evidence Hound repo provides the stack. Your private repo holds everything about your organisation.
Secrets are in neither. They live on the VM.

panel.title: Example Pty Ltd's platform
lines: A private VM, here ciso.example.com, with Docker Engine and the Compose plugin
The compliance repo at /opt/compliance, read-only, with a deploy key

steps.title: Make the secrets on the VM
narration: Make a secrets folder that only root can read.
Generate the database password and CISO Assistant's secret key straight into it.
The runner's token and the Microsoft 365 certificate start empty, and are filled later.
No secret is ever typed on a command line or committed.

terminal.command: cd /etc/evidence-hound/secrets && sudo sh -c 'umask 022; openssl rand -hex 24 > postgres_password; openssl rand -hex 32 > django_secret_key; : > hound_ca_token; : > m365_client_certificate'

steps.title: Start the stack
narration: Clone both repositories.
Link your repo's deploy settings as the stack's environment file, so your settings drive it.
Then start the stack and wait. The first start loads CISO Assistant's libraries, which takes several minutes.

terminal.command: docker compose up -d --wait postgres backend worker frontend caddy
terminal.output:
✔ Container compose-postgres-1  Healthy
 ✔ Container compose-backend-1   Healthy
 ✔ Container compose-caddy-1     Healthy

steps.title: A person signs in, and the runner gets its own token
narration: Create the first administrator, who signs in to CISO Assistant as a person.
Then create the runner's service account and its token.
The script writes the token straight into the secrets folder. It is never shown or copied.
Your turn: create the runner's token for hound-runner at example dot com.

terminal.output:
Email: grc@example.com
Password: 
Superuser created successfully.

try.prompt: Type the command that creates the runner's token for hound-runner@example.com.

steps.title: Check the config and its secrets
narration: Register the Microsoft 365 app as its guide says, and store its certificate as a secret.
Then check the config and that every secret it names resolves.
hound runs in the runner container, with your repo mounted read-only.

terminal.command: docker compose run --rm runner config validate /config/hound.yaml --check-secrets

steps.title: Apply the scope in two steps
narration: Apply the scope in two pull requests, so the first apply is small and easy to check.
First access and settings: who signs in, with which roles, and multi-factor authentication for everyone.
Then the audits. Each time, read the plan before you apply it.

terminal.command: docker compose run --rm runner scope plan /config/scope --config /config/hound.yaml
terminal.output:
+ user grc@example.com (analyst on Example Pty Ltd)
~ setting enforce_mfa: false -> true
Access review: 1 user has not turned on MFA yet.

terminal.command: docker compose run --rm runner scope apply /config/scope --config /config/hound.yaml

choice.question: Why apply access and settings before the audits?

options.text: So the first apply is small, and a mistake in who can sign in is easy to spot.
options.feedback: Yes. Two small plans are easier to read than one big one.

options.text: Because CISO Assistant refuses audits until MFA is on.
options.feedback: It does not. The order is for you: a small first plan is easy to check.

steps.title: Run once, then turn on the schedule
narration: Run the collectors once by hand, and check the status.
Then start the runner. It runs each collector on its own schedule, in your time zone.
In CISO Assistant, the rows the collectors cover now have results and evidence.

steps.title: From now on, every change is a pull request
narration: A new starter, a leaver, a setting, a collector or an upgrade: each one is a pull request to the compliance repo.
The repo's workflow scans it for secrets, validates it, and comments the scope plan on the pull request.
After the merge, a second reviewer approves the apply.

choice.question: Someone leaves Example Pty Ltd. How do you remove their access?

options.text: Remove them from scope/access.yaml in a pull request; the apply deactivates them.
options.feedback: Yes. The change is reviewed, recorded, and they are deactivated, never deleted.

options.text: Delete their account in CISO Assistant.
options.feedback: The next apply would put it back, and the change would have no record. Change the repo instead.
